articleTitle: Review: Apple's M6 MacBook Pro is good, but it's missing all the exciting stuff
summary: The article describes the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro as a $1,999 laptop with improved processor performance, more ports than the MacBook Air, and a 120 Hz ProMotion mini LED display, but without the OLED touchscreen and other design updates of Apple's flagship MacBook Pros. The reviewer questions its value, particularly for buyers who do not need the mandatory 1TB storage allotment, while highlighting its performance gains over older generations.

coreControversy.criticismOrAlarm: The reviewer argues that a $1,999 starting price is difficult to justify when the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro retains the design used since 2021 and lacks the flagship models' OLED touchscreen and other updates. The mandatory 1TB storage allotment further weakens its value for buyers who do not need it, and the reviewer questions whether its improvements over the 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air are worth $500 to $700.
coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: No regulatory dispute is stated. As historical precedents for delayed design upgrades, the article cites the 13-inch M1 and M2 MacBook Pros retaining 2016-era designs and the Touch Bar, and the entry-level tier receiving the 2021-era design only with the M3 version released in 2023.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The $1,999 starting price does not include the optional $150 nano-texture matte display upgrade.
The 1TB storage allotment is mandatory, including for buyers who do not need it.
RAM starts at 16GB, with 24GB and 32GB upgrade options; the reviewer identifies RAM as the biggest limitation for the kinds of models that run well on an M6.
The 16GB configuration is limited to 153 GB/s memory bandwidth; the 24GB and 32GB configurations receive 170 GB/s.
The tested 16GB MacBook Pro has 90 percent of the memory bandwidth of the previously tested 24GB M6 Mac mini, with slightly lower graphics/gaming results.
Despite the M6's single-core performance and larger Neural Engine, the M5 Pro's higher core count delivers stronger multi-threaded CPU performance.
The reviewed model lacks a touchscreen, OLED panel, Dynamic Island, half-pound weight reduction, and glowing Apple logo.
The suggestion that the M6 will not receive Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations is explicitly presented as rumor.
An M6 MacBook Air and future OLED touchscreen upgrades for the entry-level MacBook Pro are reviewer expectations, not confirmed product announcements.
The reviewer would not be surprised by a wait of at least two years for an OLED touchscreen on this tier; this is speculation, not a release commitment.
The article cites ongoing RAM and storage shortages as a complication for expected product progression.
The article provides no numerical power-consumption measurements, battery-life figures, camera resolution, chassis dimensions, exact weight, or shipping date.
No subscription requirements, cloud-processing dependencies, key-retention policies, or FCC approval status are stated.

avoidAdvice: Poorer fit for buyers paying $1,999 specifically to obtain Apple's newest OLED touchscreen and flagship design features, which this model lacks.
Questionable value for buyers who do not need the mandatory 1TB storage allotment or cannot justify $500 to $700 in upgrades over the 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air.
Less compelling as a performance upgrade from an M4 or M5: the reviewer expects it to feel faster, but likely not staggeringly so.
fitAdvice: Buyers seeking the cheapest Apple laptop option with a 120 Hz ProMotion display or the optional $150 nano-texture finish.
Buyers who want more ports than a MacBook Air, including HDMI, an SD card reader, and Thunderbolt 4 connectivity on both sides.
Users upgrading from an M1 or M2 MacBook Air or Pro, for whom the reviewer expects a sizable improvement noticeable in day-to-day use.
Users prioritizing sustained workloads: the reviewer expects the actively cooled MacBook Pro to retain an advantage if the fanless MacBook Air receives an M6.
